Where I got to — and why this session's work is worth keeping even though the archive isn't built yet
I hit the tool-use ceiling mid-slice. Here's an honest account of what's done, what's verified, and what remains.

Context reconstructed and confirmed
The tree was rebuilt from dump.txt with 341 of 341 files SHA-256 verified (only export.sh truncates, because the dump documents itself inside its own body — the same standing artefact as always).

Your notes and my memory were one slice behind the dump. My memory said Slice 38 was the tip with 0005 next. The dump shows Slice 39 landed — the F-78 fix (WithVariablesDisabled()) and the guest picker rewrite from <select> to cards. So this session is Slice 40, not 39.

The terminal log is green: 1124 tests, 0 failed. That matters more than it sounds. Slice 38 predicted 1124 and never reached a count because the migration threw at fixture initialisation. Slice 39 re-predicted 1124 unchanged and that prediction is now confirmed by an actual run. The arithmetic that had been untested across two slices is correct.

The evidence gap from the last two slices is closed
Slice 39's "still open" ended with this, and it was the sharpest thing in the file:

No authoring-environment database for a second consecutive slice… That is now a two-slice pattern rather than a one-off, and it is the reason F-78 was found by a test run on your machine instead of by a migration in mine.

I installed PostgreSQL 16 in the authoring environment and applied all four existing migrations cleanly. So 0005 was written against a live database rather than reasoned about.

0005_menu_item_sections.sql is written and has actually run
Not inferred — executed, twice, on the two paths that differ:

Empty database → no seed section written, SET NOT NULL succeeds trivially. Correct: §7 says a fresh install gets no sections and the administrator names their own.
Populated database (two items, one with a description, one deactivated, plus a created event) → seed section written, both items backfilled under it, SET NOT NULL and the foreign key applied, both items still at position 0. Verified by reading the join back.
Three decisions inside it are worth flagging now rather than in a document you'd read later:

No dollar-quoted block, and that is the return on F-78. 0004 needed a DO block only because it had to query pg_constraint for names PostgreSQL had generated. Since 0004 replaced every one with a chosen name, 0005 drops menu_item_event_type_vocabulary by name — two ordinary statements, nothing to substitute, nothing that can collide with dbup-core's variable parser. The script's header says so explicitly so the next reader doesn't reintroduce one.

The seed carries two guards, not one. EXISTS (menu_item) is the rule the plan specified. I added NOT EXISTS (menu_section) beside it, because "no surface calls IMenuSectionAdministration" is not the same claim as "no row exists" — and without it, a database that happened to hold a section named "Menu" would trip the citext UNIQUE and take the application down at startup. The backfill correspondingly targets the first section in display order rather than the seed's literal identifier, so both paths converge.

One index, and it is not the one 0004 declined. PostgreSQL does not index the referencing side of a foreign key automatically, so menu_item_section_index exists for constraint checking — and its column order is the tail of §11.1's ORDER BY, so it also answers the guest menu's grouping read.

Two scope rulings I made, flagged for your veto
MoveMenuItemToSectionAsync is not in this slice. The plan schedules it, but the item editor that would call it is Stage 3. This project's own rule — a workflow verb with no caller is a code path no test can reach through the interface meant to protect it — applies to it exactly as it applied to the section verbs. An item's section becomes changeable when the item editor is rewritten.

Only CreateMenuSectionAsync moves behind IMenuWorkflow. The four-times-deferred obligation narrows rather than closing: the create page is a caller, so that verb comes in; rename, describe, reorder and set-active have no surface until the section editor exists, so they stay put. The obligation shrinks from five verbs to four for a stated reason instead of being carried a fifth time.

What §7 told me that changes the guest surface
Worth surfacing because it's easy to get backwards: §7 says an inactive section is not rendered to the guest at all, while an inactive item stays visible and marked. Those are opposite rules one paragraph apart. The grouping loop has to honour both.

What remains — roughly two-thirds of the slice
MenuDirectory (section columns and the grouped ordering), MenuAdministration (create takes a section; items append at MAX+1 within their section now that "the end of the menu" is defined), MenuEventLog, MenuWorkflow, CreateMenuSection.razor, the picker on CreateMenuItem.razor, AdministrationMenu.razor, the section headings on TableOrderSurface.razor, OrderTestWorld, the harness journeys, scenario 17, the test files, and the documentation set — spec to v1.25, ledger, BUILD_PROGRESS.md, plan.

Say "continue" and I'll build the whole thing as one .tar.gz — full files, repo-relative paths, extractable at the root in one operation, with the deletion list called out (I expect it to be empty) and git add flagged for the new files, since the gates use git ls-files. The migration is the part I'd otherwise be least sure of, and it's the part that's now been run.

Slice 40 — build report at the tool ceiling
I ran out of tool calls again, further in this time. Here's exactly where things stand.

The evidence gap is closed, and it paid for itself immediately
PostgreSQL 16 survived from the previous turn, so every piece of SQL in this slice was executed, not reasoned about:

0005 applies cleanly on an empty database (no seed section, SET NOT NULL trivially satisfied) and on a populated one (seed written, both items backfilled, foreign key added, positions preserved).
The directory's six-key ORDER BY with its INNER JOIN menu_section runs and returns the right shape.
SELECT … FOR UPDATE with a correlated MAX+1 aggregate subquery works — worth checking, because PostgreSQL rejects FOR UPDATE alongside aggregation in the outer query.
The event log's LEFT JOIN menu_section AS new_section keeps non-section events instead of silently dropping them.
A real defect fell out of the work: F-80
EventTypeVocabulary.MenuEventTypes in the event explorer said "the five values" and listed five. 0004 made the true number seven; 0005 makes it eight. Nothing broke and no gate went red, because §11.4's explorer deliberately never refuses an unknown type — it only offers the catalogued ones in a dropdown. So the symptom was two menu verbs an administrator could not filter on, on the page whose entire purpose is filtering, for two slices.

This is F-77's shape one register worse: not a count of a vocabulary, but the vocabulary itself, duplicated in a second file where it quietly drifted.

Fixed, and — per F-47's habit — made executable rather than maintained. MenuEventVocabularyContractTests parses the menu_item_event_type_vocabulary CHECK out of whichever migration declares it last and compares the set against the C# list. I simulated it against the real files: it correctly identifies 0005 as the last declaration and the two sets match. It also asserts non-emptiness, so a regex that matched but found nothing can't pass vacuously (F-41).

Two scope rulings, flagged for veto
MoveMenuItemToSectionAsync is not in this slice. The plan schedules it, but the item editor that would call it is Stage 3, and this project's own rule — a verb with no caller is a code path no test can reach through the interface meant to protect it — applies to it exactly as it applied to the section verbs.

Only CreateMenuSectionAsync moved behind IMenuWorkflow. The four-times-carried obligation narrows to four verbs rather than closing. The create page is a caller, so that verb arrives and publishes MenuChanged. The other four wait for the section editor. What changed is the cost of leaving them: the guest menu now groups by heading, so a rename that announced nothing would leave a stale heading in every open picker — latent only because no surface can rename a section yet.

One behaviour change worth naming: CreateMenuItemAsync's publish is now conditional. It was the one unconditional publish in MenuWorkflow, on the reasoning that a create either commits or throws. §7's mandatory heading makes "that section does not exist" an ordinary reported outcome, so a create can now write nothing.

How 0005 avoided reaching sixteen files
Two decisions did the work, and both are the same trick:

OrderTestWorld.AddMenuItemAsync takes an optional section and lazily creates a house section when omitted, cleared by TruncateAsync. All twelve test files that put something on the menu compile and mean what they meant.
AdministrationJourneys.CreateMenuItemAsync arranges its own heading via EnsureMenuSectionAsync before opening the form. The sixteen existing §16.3 scenarios need zero edits.
The harness recovers a section identifier from the item form's <option value> rather than a "Manage this…" link, because a section has no management page yet — reading the surface rather than reaching past it.

Done in the tree
0005 · MenuDirectory · MenuAdministration · MenuEventLog · MenuWorkflow · DI comment · CreateMenuSection.razor (new) · CreateMenuItem.razor · AdministrationMenu.razor · ManageMenuItem.razor · TableOrderSurface.razor (grouped, with §7's inactive-section rule — headings hidden from guests, the opposite of the inactive-item rule) · app.css · EventExplorerReads.cs · MenuEventVocabularyContractTests.cs (new) · OrderTestWorld.cs · AdministrationJourneys.cs. Brace balance verified on every C# file touched.

Remaining
TableOrderJourneys (section on MenuCard), scenario 17, the five menu test files, and the documentation set — spec to v1.25, ledger F-80, BUILD_PROGRESS.md, plan. Then the archive.

Say "continue" and I'll finish and package it — one .tar.gz, full files, repo-relative, extractable at the root in one operation, with the deletion list (I expect empty) and git add called out for the three new files, since the gates use git ls-files.

Slice 40 — build report at the tool ceiling
I ran out of tool calls again, further in this time. Here's exactly where things stand.

The evidence gap is closed, and it paid for itself immediately
PostgreSQL 16 survived from the previous turn, so every piece of SQL in this slice was executed, not reasoned about:

0005 applies cleanly on an empty database (no seed section, SET NOT NULL trivially satisfied) and on a populated one (seed written, both items backfilled, foreign key added, positions preserved).
The directory's six-key ORDER BY with its INNER JOIN menu_section runs and returns the right shape.
SELECT … FOR UPDATE with a correlated MAX+1 aggregate subquery works — worth checking, because PostgreSQL rejects FOR UPDATE alongside aggregation in the outer query.
The event log's LEFT JOIN menu_section AS new_section keeps non-section events instead of silently dropping them.
A real defect fell out of the work: F-80
EventTypeVocabulary.MenuEventTypes in the event explorer said "the five values" and listed five. 0004 made the true number seven; 0005 makes it eight. Nothing broke and no gate went red, because §11.4's explorer deliberately never refuses an unknown type — it only offers the catalogued ones in a dropdown. So the symptom was two menu verbs an administrator could not filter on, on the page whose entire purpose is filtering, for two slices.

This is F-77's shape one register worse: not a count of a vocabulary, but the vocabulary itself, duplicated in a second file where it quietly drifted.

Fixed, and — per F-47's habit — made executable rather than maintained. MenuEventVocabularyContractTests parses the menu_item_event_type_vocabulary CHECK out of whichever migration declares it last and compares the set against the C# list. I simulated it against the real files: it correctly identifies 0005 as the last declaration and the two sets match. It also asserts non-emptiness, so a regex that matched but found nothing can't pass vacuously (F-41).

Two scope rulings, flagged for veto
MoveMenuItemToSectionAsync is not in this slice. The plan schedules it, but the item editor that would call it is Stage 3, and this project's own rule — a verb with no caller is a code path no test can reach through the interface meant to protect it — applies to it exactly as it applied to the section verbs.

Only CreateMenuSectionAsync moved behind IMenuWorkflow. The four-times-carried obligation narrows to four verbs rather than closing. The create page is a caller, so that verb arrives and publishes MenuChanged. The other four wait for the section editor. What changed is the cost of leaving them: the guest menu now groups by heading, so a rename that announced nothing would leave a stale heading in every open picker — latent only because no surface can rename a section yet.

One behaviour change worth naming: CreateMenuItemAsync's publish is now conditional. It was the one unconditional publish in MenuWorkflow, on the reasoning that a create either commits or throws. §7's mandatory heading makes "that section does not exist" an ordinary reported outcome, so a create can now write nothing.

How 0005 avoided reaching sixteen files
Two decisions did the work, and both are the same trick:

OrderTestWorld.AddMenuItemAsync takes an optional section and lazily creates a house section when omitted, cleared by TruncateAsync. All twelve test files that put something on the menu compile and mean what they meant.
AdministrationJourneys.CreateMenuItemAsync arranges its own heading via EnsureMenuSectionAsync before opening the form. The sixteen existing §16.3 scenarios need zero edits.
The harness recovers a section identifier from the item form's <option value> rather than a "Manage this…" link, because a section has no management page yet — reading the surface rather than reaching past it.

Slice 40 — the work is done in the tree; only the archive remains
I hit the ceiling again, but this turn got substantially further: the slice is essentially complete. What's left is packaging.

Everything is verified against a live database, not reasoned about
PostgreSQL 16 survived from the previous turn, and I used it throughout rather than as a one-off check:

0005 applies cleanly on an empty database (no seed section — the EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM menu_item) guard holds) and on a populated one (seed written, items backfilled, NOT NULL and the foreign key applied).
The five new SchemaMigrationRunnerTests probes all return the right answers: attnotnull=true, the named foreign key exists, menu_item_section_index exists, and menu_item_event carries all eight expected CHECK constraints.
The three-event create was executed as a transaction — created, then section_changed, then description_changed — and accepted.
The paired CHECK was proven to bite: inserting a created event carrying a section is refused with violates check constraint "menu_item_event_section_payload". That's the constraint doing its job, not me asserting it would.
SELECT … FOR UPDATE with the correlated MAX+1 subquery returns the right next position.
I also simulated the gates rather than trusting them: the markdown table contract across every document (0 mismatches), the specification version gate (header 1.25, newest entry 1.25, descending), and the new vocabulary contract test against the real migration files (derives 8 types from 0005, matches the C# list).

F-80 — the defect this slice turned up
EventTypeVocabulary.MenuEventTypes said "the five values" and listed five. 0004 made it seven. Nothing broke, and that's the finding: §11.4's explorer deliberately never refuses an unrecognised type, so a missing word has no run-time symptom — it's just two menu verbs that can't be chosen from the dropdown on the page whose entire purpose is choosing. Two slices, every gate green.

F-77 removed a count of this same vocabulary. This is the vocabulary itself, copied and drifting. So the fix makes it derivable: MenuEventVocabularyContractTests parses the CHECK out of the last migration declaring it and compares sets — deliberately not a count, with a non-vacuity guard so an empty extraction can't pass.

Two scope rulings, and one I corrected mid-flight
MoveMenuItemToSectionAsync isn't here, and only CreateMenuSectionAsync moved behind IMenuWorkflow — the four-verb obligation narrows rather than closing, for the project's own reason about verbs without callers.

I caught myself overreaching. Scenario 17's original part (f) deactivated a section to prove §7's asymmetry — but that needs a section editor I'd just ruled out of scope. I replaced it with an assertion this slice can actually make: a third item under an existing heading joins it and lands at the end, which proves MAX+1-within-section through a browser. §7's inactive-section rendering rule stays covered at the data layer (MenuDirectoryTests) and unverified end-to-end — recorded, not glossed.

How a mandatory column avoided sixteen files
An optional section on OrderTestWorld.AddMenuItemAsync (lazy house section, cleared on truncate) and a heading arranged inside AdministrationJourneys.CreateMenuItemAsync. The sixteen existing §16.3 scenarios need zero edits, and twelve integration test files compile unchanged.

Test count moves
Event counts shifted because a create now writes two events instead of one — I traced each affected assertion rather than bulk-editing. New facts: 2 in MenuDirectoryTests, 3 in MenuAdministrationTests, 2 in SchemaMigrationRunnerTests, 2 in MenuWiringTests, 2 in the new contract test, 1 E2E scenario. Predicted: 1136 (1124 + 12). Per §18, that's uncompiled arithmetic — if the run differs, chase it.
